text: Deltas can also form during a relative fall in sea level; these are often referred to as “lowstand” or “shelf-margin” deltas or systems tracts (Figs. 5.18 and 5.19). text: ### 9.4.1 Processes and Deposits
excerpt: 9.4.1 Processes and Deposits

text: The Mississippi River Delta (Fig. 9.13) has long been considered the “type” river-dominated delta (Fig. 9.5). Strong waves and currents do not impinge upon its protected shoreline, so sediment deposited at and near the shore zone is not reworked or dispersed laterally (Figs. 9.4 and 9.7). With time and sufficient accommodation space between the sea surface and seafloor to accept sediment, such a delta will prograde seaward (Fig. 9.9), as will the delta zones (Fig. 9.7). By that process, surfaces representing instants in geologic time crosscut boundaries between sedimentary facies (see the time lines or clinoforms in Fig. 9.9). However, over time, progradation and vertical aggradation lead to a progressive shallowing of the water depth, to the point at which the main river(s) feeding sediment to its delta will shift toward deeper water (toward lower points on the seafloor), thereby causing the distributary-channel switching discussed earlier (Fig. 9.11). During the past 4600 years, there have been no fewer than eight periods of channel and lobe switching on the Mississippi River Delta (Fig. 9.12).

text: In Prudhoe Bay field, formative processes of distributary mouth bars were evaluated by Tye and Hickey (2001). A 1000-ft. (300-m) horizontal well was drilled into a distributary mouth-bar reservoir sandstone, and three cores were obtained. Seven sandy lithofacies were identified in the core, all are moderately to very well sorted and fine to very fine-grained. Six of the lithofacies exhibit average horizontal permeabilities of 12–40 md. The seventh, best-sorted lithofacies averages 129 md. The origin of these lithofacies was determined by studying modern river-dominated delta processes and sediments. Geoscientists believe that sediment plumes emanating from distributary channels during flood stage deposited the best-sorted and most-permeable sands (the seventh lithofacies) at the apex or most-proximal part of the distributary mouth bars, as well as along the proximal-bar margin (Fig. 9.16). Finer-grained, more poorly sorted sands and muds were deposited more distally, under lower flow-regime conditions.

text: General geology of Prudhoe Bay field, Alaska, in the river-dominated deltaic deposits of the ancient Sagavanirktok River, was discussed in Chapter 7. The most prolific reservoir rocks in the field are of fluvial, braided-river origin. The lower stratigraphic interval, called the Romeo Zone (Figs. 9.16–9.18), is composed mainly of river-dominated delta-front and prodelta deposits (Fig. 7.22 and 7.23, and Fig. 9.17) that in recent years have been targeted for production, mainly from horizontal wells (Tye and Hickey, 2001; Tye et al., 1999). Productive deltaic facies are distributary-channel and distributary mouth-bar sandstones (Figs. 9.18 and 9.19). text: ### 9.4.3 Kuparuk River Field, Alaska USA
excerpt: 9.4.3 Kuparuk River Field, Alaska USA

text: A similar example is provided by the Cretaceous Kuparuk River field on the North Slope of Alaska. This is the second largest oil field in North America, with 6BBSTOOIP. As of 2006, 2BBO had been produced. Production is from two intervals, named the A and C units. In the early days of field development each unit was considered a laterally continuous sandstone body. However, sequence stratigraphy correlations revealed that the A unit consists of six separate sandstone bodies that prograded in the seaward (northeast) direction, each separated by a high-frequency transgressive marine shale (Fig. 9.25).

text: ### 9.5.1 Processes and Deposits
excerpt: 9.5.1 Processes and Deposits

text: Along a coast that is unprotected from waves and ocean currents, sediment that reaches the shoreline is dispersed laterally (Figs. 9.4 and 9.6). If sufficient sand is supplied to the shoreline, over time, the shore zone will accrete laterally and prograde basinward. The sequential development of a wave-influenced shoreline is illustrated in Fig. 9.26. In this case, the linear shoreline is fed by longshore drift; not only does the shoreline prograde and accrete laterally, but also is the river mouth progressively deflected in the direction of longshore drift.
